title: What is the PostgreSQL equivalent of Oracle's `CLOB` data type (`TEXT`)?
shortTitle: PostgreSQL Equivalent of Oracle's CLOB Data Type (TEXT)

s1_definition.profdef: Oracle's `CLOB` (Character Large OBject) stores very large variable-length character data — up to about 4GB — using special large-object storage and locator-based access. The PostgreSQL equivalent is simply `TEXT`, a native variable-length character type with no declared length limit (practically up to about 1GB per value), used and indexed like any ordinary string column without special locator APIs.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India storing a customer's long complaint letter or the full text of a loan agreement. In Oracle you would put that in a special oversized drawer called a `CLOB` that needs its own handling procedure. In PostgreSQL you just use a `TEXT` column — the same drawer you use for a short name works for a whole book, so there is no separate special drawer to manage.
s1_definition.oneliner: Oracle's `CLOB` maps to PostgreSQL's `TEXT` — a plain, unlimited-length string type you read and write like any normal column.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Oracle's `CLOB` (Character Large OBject) stores very large variable-length character data — up to about 4GB — using special large-object storage and locator-based access. The PostgreSQL equivalent is simply `TEXT`, a native variable-length character type with no declared length limit (practically up to about 1GB per value), used and indexed like any ordinary string column without special locator APIs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India storing a customer's long complaint letter or the full text of a loan agreement. In Oracle you would put that in a special oversized drawer called a `CLOB` that needs its own handling procedure. In PostgreSQL you just use a `TEXT` column — the same drawer you use for a short name works for a whole book, so there is no separate special drawer to manage.

**One line to remember:** Oracle's `CLOB` maps to PostgreSQL's `TEXT` — a plain, unlimited-length string type you read and write like any normal column.

sections.s2_technical:
Oracle distinguishes small strings (`VARCHAR2`, capped at 4000 bytes or 32767 with extended strings) from large character data (`CLOB`), which stores up to roughly 4GB. A `CLOB` is accessed through a LOB locator, and older code often used `DBMS_LOB` procedures or streaming APIs to read and write it piece by piece. This split means Oracle developers must decide up front whether a column is "small text" or "large text."

PostgreSQL does not need that split. Its `TEXT` type is a variable-length string with no length declaration and a practical ceiling of about 1GB per value. Importantly, `VARCHAR(n)`, `VARCHAR` without a length, and `TEXT` are all the same underlying type in PostgreSQL — the only difference is the optional length check. Large values are automatically moved out-of-line into TOAST (The Oversized-Attribute Storage Technique) storage and transparently compressed, so you never manage locators manually. You `SELECT`, `INSERT`, concatenate, and pattern-match a `TEXT` column exactly like a short string.

For migration from Oracle to PostgreSQL, the standard mapping is `CLOB → TEXT`, `VARCHAR2 → VARCHAR` or `TEXT`, `NCLOB → TEXT`, and `BLOB → BYTEA` for binary. A senior nuance is that PostgreSQL also has a separate "large object" facility (`lo_*` functions with `oid` references) that more closely mirrors Oracle's locator style for streaming multi-gigabyte files, but for ordinary large text you almost always want `TEXT`, not large objects, because `TEXT` is simpler, transactional, and directly queryable. You can even add a GIN full-text index on a `TEXT` column, which Oracle `CLOB` cannot do without Oracle Text.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India is migrating its complaints system from Oracle to PostgreSQL. The old schema stored the full complaint narrative in a `CLOB` column and access code used LOB locators. During migration the team must map each Oracle type to its PostgreSQL equivalent and confirm that long narratives still store and read correctly without any special handling.

Our mini-project builds a small `TypeMappingService` that maps Oracle column types to PostgreSQL types and a `ComplaintRepository` simulation that stores and retrieves a very long complaint narrative in a `TEXT`-style field, proving that a multi-kilobyte string round-trips exactly like a short one — no locator, no streaming API.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one complaint with a short name and a roughly 5000-character narrative that in Oracle would have required a `CLOB`.

Step 1 — The mapping service is asked what Oracle `CLOB` becomes in PostgreSQL and answers `TEXT`, and that `BLOB` becomes `BYTEA`. This is the migration rule the whole answer rests on.

Step 2 — A long narrative is built by repeating a sentence 100 times, producing a multi-kilobyte string, far beyond a `VARCHAR2(4000)` limit but trivial for `TEXT`.

Step 3 — The repository saves the complaint with a plain put, standing in for a plain `INSERT`. In real PostgreSQL this is one ordinary statement with no `DBMS_LOB` calls and no locator.

Step 4 — The complaint is read back with a plain get, standing in for a plain `SELECT`, and the full narrative comes back as an ordinary `String`.

Step 5 — The demo confirms the loaded narrative equals the original exactly, proving a CLOB-sized value round-trips through a `TEXT`-style column with no special handling.

Final output:

```text
Oracle CLOB  -> PostgreSQL TEXT
Oracle BLOB  -> PostgreSQL BYTEA
Stored narrative length = 6300 chars
Round-trip intact (no locator needed) = true
```

```text
  Oracle schema                PostgreSQL schema
  ─────────────                ─────────────────
  narrative CLOB   ──map──▶     narrative TEXT
  photo     BLOB   ──map──▶     photo     BYTEA
        │
        ▼ (migration)
  long String (~6KB)
        │  save() = plain INSERT (no DBMS_LOB)
        ▼
  [ TEXT column ]  ──TOAST──▶ stored/compressed out-of-line transparently
        │  findById() = plain SELECT
        ▼
  full String returned, equals original
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The PostgreSQL equivalent of Oracle's `CLOB` is `TEXT`. In Oracle, `CLOB` is a special large-character type holding up to about 4GB, accessed through a LOB locator and often manipulated with `DBMS_LOB` procedures, which forces developers to split columns into "small text" (`VARCHAR2`) and "large text" (`CLOB`). PostgreSQL removes that split: `TEXT` is a native variable-length string with no declared length and a practical ceiling of about 1GB, and crucially `VARCHAR(n)`, unbounded `VARCHAR`, and `TEXT` are the same underlying type, differing only by an optional length check. You read and write a `TEXT` column with ordinary `SELECT` and `INSERT` — no locator and no streaming API — and PostgreSQL transparently moves large values out-of-line into TOAST storage and compresses them.

For a migration, the mapping I state is `CLOB → TEXT`, `NCLOB → TEXT`, `VARCHAR2 → VARCHAR` or `TEXT`, and `BLOB → BYTEA` for binary data. At the National Bank of India, when we migrated the complaints system from Oracle to PostgreSQL, the complaint narratives that had lived in `CLOB` columns simply became `TEXT`, and the locator-based access code collapsed into plain queries, which also let us add a GIN full-text index for searching complaints — something the Oracle `CLOB` could not do without Oracle Text. A senior nuance I always mention is that PostgreSQL also has a separate large-object facility using `oid` references and `lo_*` functions that mirrors Oracle's streaming locator style for truly huge binary files, but for ordinary large text you should prefer `TEXT` because it is simpler, fully transactional, and directly queryable and indexable. The line I always state is that Oracle `CLOB` becomes PostgreSQL `TEXT`, a plain unlimited-length string you treat like any normal column.
